name: Outstanding Withdrawals
observation: The catalogue carousel, re-timed from ~114s to one revolution in ~19s (seeded 17-22s), so a full survey of the ring costs one patient look-around rather than two minutes. The ring is no longer full. Of the 48 slots on the rail, four RUNS OF SLOTS ARE EMPTY - four holes of visibly different sizes turning past the player. Beside each hole sits exactly one card carrying the violet bar, now stencilled WITHDRAWN instead of PREFIX; those four CHARGE CARDS are the only violet cards on the rail. Every card, charge or not, carries one large three-digit CALL NUMBER in the top field (0.11m glyphs - legible right across the room, and the player can walk to within a metre of the ring's near side). The rail torus gets a notch map: 48 evenly spaced tick marks, one per slot, so an empty run is literally countable - "this hole is six notches wide" - instead of being judged by arc length. Static and readable at leisure: the 20 shelf-edge strips on the west and east stacks, each now reading CODE / a 48-number range / a one-word section name, e.g. "CE  673-720  UPDRAFT".
deduction:
Three linked noticings, none of them a transcription.

1. THE HOLES BELONG TO THE CHARGE CARDS. Every violet card has an empty run touching it and nothing else on the ring does. A charge card is what a library leaves in the drawer when entries are taken out; the hole beside it is what was taken. So the ring is not damaged - it is a file with four items on loan.

2. THE HOLES ARE COUNTABLE, AND THAT COUNT IS AN IDENTITY. The notches on the rail mean each hole has an exact size (2 to 7). No two holes are the same size. That is the "oh, THAT's what's happening" moment, and it is the one the key triggers: the numbers on the neighbour's slip are not positions, shifts or ordinals - they are how many entries each withdrawal took, which is the number of empty notches. Until the slip is read aloud, four numbers of unknown meaning; the moment it is, the player is looking straight at the four things they name.

3. A CALL NUMBER IS AN ADDRESS IN THIS ROOM. Each charge card shows a three-digit number and no letter block. The shelf strips each state a 48-number range, so exactly one strip in the room contains that number, and that strip names the section the entry was filed under. Cross-referencing a number against the stacks is what this room is for; the shelves stop being wallpaper and become the decoding table.

The player therefore ends up with four (hole size -> section word) pairs held simultaneously, e.g. six-notch -> UPDRAFT, and can go no further alone.
answerFormat: 4 letters (safe alphabet: A-Z minus I, O, S), e.g. DUVE
neighbourKeyRole: Printed in the neighbour's Fragment as: label "REQUEST SLIP - ENTRIES PER WITHDRAWAL", value "3-6-2-4". The label is the interpreter and the value is the order. It contains no letter, no call number and no section name - held by a player who cannot see the ring it is four meaningless digits, and it can never be the answer. What it does is two things the Archive player provably cannot do alone: (a) it declares that a withdrawal is named by HOW MANY entries it took, which is what converts the four holes from scenery into labelled identifiers, and (b) it fixes the reading order of the four sections (24 permutations, punished by the existing wrong-answer lockout). Conversely the slip is worthless in reverse: the neighbour learns nothing about the Archive from holding it. Note for the builder: the semantic sits in the KEY LABEL deliberately, so the interpretive step arrives over the voice call rather than off the Archive player's own panel.
seededValues: Revolution period, integer 17-22s, and rotation direction (+/-)
The four withdrawal sizes: 4 distinct values drawn from {2,3,4,5,6,7}, total empty slots <= 18
The four charge-card slot indices on the 48-slot ring, constrained so >= 5 occupied slots separate the end of one withdrawal group from the start of the next
Which side of its hole each charge card sits on (leading or trailing)
The 20 shelf strips: section word per strip, drawn from a pool so that all 20 initials are distinct and none is I, O or S (the 48-wide ranges 001-048 ... 913-960 stay fixed by strip index)
The four charge-card call numbers: one per distinct shelf strip, at least 6 clear of either end of its range so no boundary is ambiguous
The remaining ~29 decoy call numbers (all unique, none equal to a charge number) and their decoy 3-letter blocks
The 18 drawer codes (flavour only, reshuffled per session)
The slip permutation - the neighbour's key

geometryChanges.change: Re-time the carousel: delete the fixed CARD_RATE = 0.055 and drive the ring from the seeded period. CRITICAL: replace `carouselGroup.rotation.y += dt * CARD_RATE` with an assignment, `carouselGroup.rotation.y = dir * (elapsed % period) / period * Math.PI * 2`. The current += accumulation is frame-rate dependent and drifts between clients, which breaks constraint 4 today regardless of this puzzle. `elapsed` should be derived from the shared run start (Date.now() - runStartedAt), not per-client mount time.
Sparse ring: build the cardQuads array from the seeded slot layout - ~33 of 48 quads instead of 48 - leaving the four empty runs. Same makeAtlasQuads call, same merged mesh, same material.
geometryChanges.cost: Re-uses existing mesh; ~30% fewer triangles. 0 draw calls.

geometryChanges.change: Card atlas redraw (makeCardAtlas): the big top field becomes a three-digit CALL NUMBER instead of the slot index; the violet bar is relabelled WITHDRAWN and appears only on the four seeded charge cards (drop the `i % 8 === 3` rule); non-charge cards keep the 3-letter block as decoy. BLK/DC- flavour lines unchanged.
geometryChanges.cost: Same canvas, same texture, same draw call.

geometryChanges.change: Notch map on the rail: give the existing TorusGeometry material a 1024x16 emissive strip map of 48 tick marks (repeat 1 around the ring, aligned to slot centres). This is what makes an empty run countable rather than estimated, and it is the single highest-value change for solvability.
geometryChanges.cost: 1 small texture on an existing mesh. 0 draw calls, 0 lights.

geometryChanges.cost: Same label atlas, same draw call.

geometryChanges.change: Nothing is added, raised or occluded. No new geometry, no new lights, no clickable object. All puzzle text stays where it already is: shelf strips at 0.125-1.90m, card ink at 2.36-2.88m on a ring the player can walk to within ~1m of. The rail notches are non-text.

fragmentBrief:
CIRCULATION — OUTSTANDING WITHDRAWALS

Four charge cards are still out on the rail. Each one stands
where entries were taken out of the file. Nothing leaves this
room without leaving its place behind.

A call number is an address. Every strip on these shelves
states the range it holds.

REPORT: four letters — the initial of the section each
withdrawal was filed under, in the order the desk asks for.

The desk's request slip is in your neighbour's chamber.
exampleWalkthrough:
SESSION SEED PRODUCES:
period 19s, direction +. Widths {6, 2, 4, 3}. Layout on the 48 slots (charge card first, then its empty run):
  W-A: charge at slot 4,  empty 5-10   (6 notches)
  W-B: charge at slot 16, empty 17-18  (2 notches)
  W-C: charge at slot 27, empty 28-31  (4 notches)
  W-D: charge at slot 39, empty 40-42  (3 notches)
  Occupied normal slots: 0-3, 11-15, 19-26, 32-38, 43-47 = 29 cards. 29 + 4 charge + 15 empty = 48. Separations between groups: 5, 8, 7, 9 - no two holes can be confused for one.

SHELF STRIPS (extract of the 20, all initials distinct, none I/O/S):
  AA 001-048 MANIFEST   AB 049-096 ROTATION   AC 097-144 HULLPLATE
  AD 145-192 COOLANT    AE 193-240 BALLAST    BA 241-288 VALVES
  BB 289-336 GAUGES     BC 337-384 FUSEBOX    BD 385-432 DOWELS
  BE 433-480 TUMBLERS   CA 481-528 ALMANAC    CB 529-576 PARALLAX
  CC 577-624 NADIRLOG   CD 625-672 LEDGERS    CE 673-720 UPDRAFT
  DA 721-768 QUARRY     DB 769-816 KEYSTONE   DC 817-864 WARDEN
  DD 865-912 EMBERS     DE 913-960 XENOLITH

CHARGE CARD CALL NUMBERS: W-A 702, W-B 254, W-C 878, W-D 411.

WHAT THE PLAYER DOES:
1. Stands under the ring. It turns a full circle in 19 seconds, so in one turn she sees the whole file. She notices four gaps, and that each gap has a violet WITHDRAWN card against it - the only violet cards up there.
2. She counts the rail notches across each gap as it comes round: six, two, four, three. Reading the charge card beside each as it passes: 702, 254, 878, 411. (One number per pass, ~0.11m glyphs; she can stand a metre under the ring's near side to catch the awkward one.)
3. She walks the stacks with those four numbers. 702 falls inside 673-720 -> CE UPDRAFT. 254 -> BA VALVES. 878 -> DD EMBERS. 411 -> BD DOWELS. She now holds: six->UPDRAFT, two->VALVES, four->EMBERS, three->DOWELS. She has four letters and no order, and no reason yet to think the counts mean anything.
4. Over the call, the Engine Room player reads her Fragment: "REQUEST SLIP - ENTRIES PER WITHDRAWAL: three, six, two, four." That is the moment - the slip is naming the holes by how big they are.
5. She applies it: 3 -> DOWELS -> D. 6 -> UPDRAFT -> U. 2 -> VALVES -> V. 4 -> EMBERS -> E.
6. She types DUVE. Lock opens.

SERVER/CLIENT CONTRACT NOTES FOR THE BUILDER:
- puzzles.js must become chamber-aware: BUILDERS keyed by chamberId (archive -> buildWithdrawals) rather than by an alternating type list, since the puzzle is now made of the room.
- Put the layout generator in one shared module (e.g. shared/archive-layout.js) imported by both server/puzzles.js and public/js/rooms/archive.js, taking a single 32-bit `seed` and returning {period, dir, slots[], charges[{slot,width,call}], strips[]}. The server derives `answer` from it; the client renders from it. The seed travels in prompt (prompt.kind = 'withdrawals', prompt.seed, prompt.instruction, prompt.answerLength = 4). The answer itself is never sent - same posture as the existing cipherText.
- key = { kind: 'slip', label: 'REQUEST SLIP - ENTRIES PER WITHDRAWAL', value: '3-6-2-4' }.
- wouldSolve() needs a branch for kind 'slip': it returns false against any prompt whose kind is not 'withdrawals', and for a 'withdrawals' prompt it must return true only if the slip's widths match that chamber's own layout - i.e. the existing "nobody holds the key to their own prompt" repair pass keeps working.
- hud.js renderFragment needs a 'withdrawals' branch: print fragmentBrief text, set fragNeedLabel to 'request slip'.
difficultyNotes:
WHY A 13-YEAR-OLD CAN GET THIS: every operation is primary-school - count notches in a gap, check whether 702 sits between 673 and 720, take the first letter of a word, put four letters in a given order. No cipher, no astronomy, no arithmetic beyond comparison. The fiction does the teaching: a card left where something was borrowed is a familiar idea, and the phrase "entries per withdrawal" explains itself the instant you are looking at holes of different sizes.

WHAT STOPS IT BEING INSTANT: (1) the ring must actually be watched - four charge cards spread ~90 degrees apart on a 19s revolution means one full patient turn minimum, more to double-check a count, and the numbers cannot all be caught in one glance; (2) the holes have to be read as meaningful rather than as damage, which nothing on the Archive's own panel says; (3) the four shelf strips have to be hunted out of 20 spread across both stack walls, which means walking the room and reading, not standing at the panel; (4) the order is genuinely unobtainable alone - 24 permutations against the wrong-answer lockout is not a viable brute force, and even a player who guessed one would not know which hole the slip's leading digit meant.

THE PERCEPTION RISK, AND ITS FIX: at 19s per revolution a card passes a fixed bearing every 0.40s, so nothing that requires reading many cards in sequence would work. This design only ever asks the player to read FOUR cards, each trackable by eye, plus static shelf text read at leisure. The one remaining risk was judging a hole's width by arc length (is that five or six?); the 48 rail notches remove it entirely and cost nothing. Minimum width is 2 so no hole is a single-frame blink, and no two widths in a session are equal.

FAILURE MODES CHECKED: a charge card can never touch two holes (>= 5 occupied slots between groups); a call number is never within 6 of a range boundary; all four charge numbers land in four different strips; all 20 section initials are distinct so a number resolves to exactly one letter; the safe alphabet excludes I, O and S so the typed answer survives being said aloud.
